dialog.body: City Clerk's office, this is Owen. How can I help you?
Good morning, Mr. Haskell. My name is Ivone Varela. I would like to inquire about a matter concerning a dog in my neighborhood.
Okay. Sure. Let me, um, let me get a pen. Alright, go ahead. What's going on with the dog?
A neighbor's dog keeps getting loose. It has happened several times in the past few weeks. The dog leaves the yard and walks along the street, and sometimes it comes onto my property.
I see. And is it, is the dog aggressive at all? Or just wandering around?
So far it has only wandered. It has barked at me once when I was taking out my trash, but it did not attempt to bite. I would simply like to prevent a problem before one occurs.
That makes sense. Okay. Have you spoken with the owner at all?
I have not spoken with them at length. I mentioned it once at the mailbox, and the gentleman said he would fix the gate. It has not been fixed, as far as I can tell.
Which brings me to my question. I would like to know who responds to this kind of complaint. Is it the police department, or is there a separate animal control officer?

Good question. Let me think how to say this. Animal control is handled through the police department here in Newport. So there's an animal control officer, and that's who would follow up on a loose dog.
I see. So I would not contact your office directly to file the complaint.

Well, you can tell me about it, and I can take down what you've told me. But the one who actually responds is the animal control officer. I can transfer you over to the police department's non-emergency line if you like. That way it gets to the right person.
Yes, I would appreciate that. Before you do, may I ask whether I will need to provide the name of the neighbor?
It helps if you know the address where the dog lives. A name is good too, but the address is the main thing. They'll ask you where the dog is getting out and what it looks like.
Understood. It is a large brown dog, I believe a mixed breed, with a white patch on its chest. I know the house, though I do not know the number offhand. I can describe it by the street.
That should be fine. They can work with a description. And, um, will you be okay giving them your name, or did you want to stay anonymous?
I am willing to give my name. I would prefer it not be shared with the neighbor, if that is possible.
I can't speak for exactly how they handle that, so I'd ask them when you get them on the line. Tell them that up front.
That is sensible. Thank you. I will do so.
Sure. Now, while I have you, is there anything else? Is the dog licensed, do you know? Some people ask about that.
I do not know whether it is licensed. I have not seen a tag, but I have not been close enough to look carefully.
That's fine. Don't get close to check. Just let the officer know you're not sure.

I will. I will also admit, Mr. Haskell, that I am a little embarrassed to be calling about something so small. I overspent on holiday gifts this year, and I have been trying to keep my head down and my budget tight, so I would rather not be involved in a dispute that might lead to any cost.
Oh, no, no, you're fine. Calling to report a loose dog isn't going to cost you anything. It's a normal thing to report.
That is a relief. Thank you for clarifying.
Okay. So, let me get you over to the police non-emergency line. It might ring a few times. If it goes to a menu, you'd want the option for animal control or just ask the person who answers.
Very well. And if the call is disconnected during the transfer, should I call back to your office or call the police directly?
Good point. If it drops, just call the police department's regular non-emergency number. It's listed on the city website. Or call me back and I'll try again.
Thank you. I will do one or the other. I appreciate your patience, Mr. Haskell.
No problem at all, Ms. Varela. Hold on one moment and I'll connect you. [pause] Okay, it's ringing for you now.
Thank you. Good day.
